newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian finmin wants a strong, broad euro.
newsitem.headline: Austrian finmin wants a strong, broad euro.

text.p: Austria's new Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger said on Friday he believed in a strong euro that would include as many European Union (EU) member states as possible when it was launched in 1999.

Edlinger, a former City of Vienna finance chief who switched to the treasury in January, said the EU should not under-estimate the problems of integrating stragglers into the planned single European currency.

"I believe it would be good if as many countries as possible were there from the start because we will have to work out how others can join. That can be complicated," Edlinger, 56, told Reuters in an interview.

The career politician, whose involvement with the ruling Social Democrats stretches back over three decades, said he was opposed to any watering down of the Maastricht Treaty's strict rules. But he said the future single currency should not be viewed as an extension of the German mark.
"I want to see a hard currency...(but) I do not imagine it as a larger German mark region," he said, speaking from his office in one of Vienna's most imposing palaces.
Based on 1997 budget projections, Edlinger said he was confident that Austria would qualify for the single currency and he vowed to maintain a firm grip on public spending in the coming years.

"If the economy grows at the expected 1.2-1.6 percent this year, it is possible to reach the Maastricht goal...(And) it is our aim to keep the overall budget deficit well within Maastricht limits in the future," he said.
A heavy smoker, Edlinger took on the most difficult job in the coalition government when Viktor Klima was promoted from finance minister to chancellor.

His first task will be negotiating the 1998 and 1999 budgets with ministers from his own party and the conservative People's Party. Talks are scheduled to start in March and Klima wants the budget signed and sealed by the end of the summer.
"I am a consensus politician. I don't want to wade in to the various ministries, it is up to the ministers to meet their targets," Edlinger said.
He forecast the government's budget deficit would narrow to 2.3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1999 from 2.5 percent in 1998 and 2.7 percent this year.
The overall budget deficit, including regional government, would not exceed 3.0 percent in 1997, down from roughly 4.0 percent in 1996, he continued.

Edlinger will need all his political skill to win support for his plans. Two years ago a row over the budget caused an irreparable split in the left-right coalition, plunging Austria into a snap general election.

He will also need to think on his feet to carry out this year's planned sale of the state's 19 percent stake in Bank Austria. The government is still recovering from its six-year battle to privatise another bank, Creditanstalt-Bankverein.

"The sale of the Bank Austria stake certainly won't take six years. Then again in 1991 when parliament passed the privatisation law on Creditanstalt, no one thought that would take six years," he said.
A self-proclaimed socialist, Edlinger favoured maintaining an Austrian influence in key industries.

"I am in favour of a speedy solution, but not any solution. At the end of the day we are dealing with a valuable asset...It makes sound political sense to keep strategic interests in Austria," he said.

As finance chief of the City of Vienna, which indirectly controls Bank Austria through its AVZ foundation, he played a crucial role in winning backing for the sale of Creditanstalt to its closest rival Bank Austria.
"I wanted Austria to have a medium-sized bank by European standards, with the focus of its interest in Vienna," he said.
